artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: When a sodium atom loses one outer electron, its 11 protons outnumber its 10 remaining electrons, so the particle becomes Na+.
artifacts.transferable_principle: A positive ion forms when electron loss leaves more protons than electrons.

steps.name: Neutral sodium
steps.beat: Start with a sodium atom where proton count and electron count balance, so the atom has no overall charge.

steps.name: Outer electron leaves
steps.beat: The single valence electron is removed from the outer shell while the nucleus stays unchanged.

steps.name: Counts become unequal
steps.beat: Sodium still has 11 protons, but now only 10 electrons remain.

steps.name: Na+ forms
steps.beat: The extra positive proton charge gives the ion a +1 charge, written as Na+.

key_symbols.meaning: The starting particle with balanced protons and electrons.
The electron being removed from the atom.
The change that reduces the electron count by one.
The resulting cation with one more proton than electron.
The charge caused by the proton-electron imbalance.

interactivity_hooks: Toggle the lost outer electron on and off to compare neutral sodium with Na+.
Click proton and electron counters to highlight why the charge changes.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: When a chlorine atom gains one electron to complete its valence shell, its 18 electrons outnumber its 17 protons, so the particle becomes Cl-.
artifacts.transferable_principle: A negative ion forms when electron gain leaves more electrons than protons.

steps.name: Neutral chlorine
steps.beat: Begin with a chlorine atom whose proton and electron counts are equal.

steps.name: Electron joins
steps.beat: One electron is added to the valence shell so the outer shell becomes complete.

steps.name: Electrons outnumber protons
steps.beat: Chlorine still has 17 protons, but now has 18 electrons.

steps.name: Cl- forms
steps.beat: The extra electron gives the ion a -1 charge, written as Cl-.

key_symbols.meaning: The starting particle before electron gain.
The added electron that changes the charge balance.
The incomplete outer shell before gain.
The resulting anion with one more electron than proton.
The charge caused by the proton-electron imbalance.

interactivity_hooks: Drag one electron into chlorine's outer shell to watch the charge counter become -1.
Toggle before and after states to compare atom and anion.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: Isotopes keep the same proton and electron counts, so their chemical reactions stay the same, but different neutron counts change their masses and mass-related physical properties.
artifacts.transferable_principle: Chemical properties follow electron arrangement, while physical properties can change when mass changes.

steps.name: Same element
steps.beat: Two atoms are shown with the same number of protons, so they are atoms of the same element.

steps.name: Same electrons
steps.beat: Their electron arrangements match, so they undergo the same chemical reactions and form compounds with the same formula.

steps.name: Different neutrons
steps.beat: The nuclei contain different numbers of neutrons, creating slightly different masses.

steps.name: Property split
steps.beat: Chemical properties remain similar, while physical properties such as density can differ.

key_symbols.meaning: The shared feature responsible for similar chemical properties.
The differing feature that changes mass.
The same reaction outcome caused by the same electron arrangement.
The physical difference caused by neutron count.
Two atoms of the same element being compared.

interactivity_hooks: Toggle neutron count while keeping electrons fixed to see which property labels change.
Compare chemical and physical property panels side by side.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: Chlorine's relative atomic mass is 35.5 because chlorine-35 contributes 75% of the weighted average and chlorine-37 contributes 25%.
artifacts.transferable_principle: Relative atomic mass is a weighted average of isotope masses using their percentage abundances.

steps.name: Two isotopes
steps.beat: Chlorine exists as chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 rather than as atoms with 35.5 nucleons.

steps.name: Different abundances
steps.beat: The sample has more chlorine-35 atoms, represented as 75%, and fewer chlorine-37 atoms, represented as 25%.

steps.name: Weight each mass
steps.beat: Multiply each isotope mass by its abundance: 35 x 75% and 37 x 25%.

steps.name: Add contributions
steps.beat: The weighted contributions add to 35.5, giving chlorine's relative atomic mass.

key_symbols.meaning: The more abundant isotope contributing most of the average.
The less abundant heavier isotope that pulls the average upward.
The combined calculation using mass and percentage abundance.
The relative atomic mass shown on the periodic table.
The source data for isotope abundance.

interactivity_hooks: Adjust abundance sliders for chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 to see the weighted average move.
Click each isotope group to reveal its individual contribution to 35.5.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: For neutral oganesson-294, the lower number 118 gives both protons and electrons, while neutrons are found by subtracting 118 from the nucleon number 294.
artifacts.transferable_principle: In nuclide notation, proton number identifies protons and neutral-atom electrons, while nucleon number minus proton number gives neutrons.

steps.name: Read the lower number
steps.beat: The proton number is 118, so an atom of oganesson contains 118 protons.

steps.name: Use neutrality
steps.beat: Because the question asks about an atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons.

steps.name: Subtract for neutrons
steps.beat: The nucleon number is 294, so neutrons are 294 - 118 = 176.

steps.name: Choose statement C
steps.beat: The correct statement is that it contains 118 protons and 176 neutrons.

key_symbols.meaning: The number that determines protons and neutral-atom electrons.
The total number of protons and neutrons.
The calculation used to find neutrons.
Distractors that confuse electrons, protons, and nucleons.
The statement matching the particle counts.

interactivity_hooks: Click each answer option to see which count rule it violates.
Reveal proton, electron, and neutron counts one at a time from the notation.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: A 2- ion with electronic structure 2,8,8 has 18 electrons after gaining two, so the neutral atom had 16 electrons and proton number 16.
artifacts.transferable_principle: To work backward from a negative ion, subtract gained electrons from the ion's electron count to find the neutral atom's proton number.

steps.name: Count ion electrons
steps.beat: The electronic structure 2,8,8 totals 18 electrons in the ion.

steps.name: Interpret 2- charge
steps.beat: A 2- ion formed when the atom gained two electrons.

steps.name: Reverse the gain
steps.beat: Subtract the gained electrons: 18 - 2 = 16 electrons in the neutral atom.

steps.name: Match proton number
steps.beat: A neutral atom with 16 electrons has 16 protons, so the option with proton number 16 is correct.

key_symbols.meaning: The ion's electron arrangement and total electron count.
The clue that two electrons were gained.
The reasoning step that removes the gained electrons to recover the neutral atom.
The matching neutral atom proton number.
The options filtered by proton number.

interactivity_hooks: Click the 2, 8, and 8 shell labels to build the total of 18 electrons.
Toggle ion charge between 1- and 2- to see how the neutral proton number changes.
Select each option to test whether its proton number matches the reversed count.
